PAGE 1 OF 9: THE CELL

**Subject:** Integrated Science  
**Grade:** 8  
**Topic:** 2.1 The Cell  
**Subtopic:** The Cell

### Comprehensive concept explanation

Cells make up the structure of living organisms and carry out various biological processes. Organisms such as amoeba are composed of a single cell hence are said to be unicellular. Organisms such as plants and animals are composed of many cells hence are said to be multicellular.

Therefore, a cell is defined as the basic unit of structure and functions in organisms. To observe the cell, a powerful magnifying instrument called a microscope is used. A microscope enlarges the image of objects when observed and improves the resolution of the image. Keep the definitions precise, and notice how each idea connects to the example that follows.

Plant and animal cell structures as seen under a light microscope. The following diagram shows the components of a plant cell as seen under a light microscope. Use the practice questions to test whether you can apply the idea, not only recall the wording.

PAGE 4 OF 9: ANIMAL CELLS USUALLY DO NOT HAVE VACUOLES, HOWEVER, SMALL TEMPORARY VACUOLES MAY OCCUR

**Subject:** Integrated Science  
**Grade:** 8  
**Topic:** 2.1 The Cell  
**Subtopic:** Animal cells usually do not have vacuoles, however, small temporary vacuoles may occur

### Comprehensive concept explanation

Similarities between a plant cell and an animal cell. They both have the cell membrane. Both have nucleus within them. Functions of the cell structures found in plants and animals’ cells. Part/structure. Understanding this clearly helps you explain the science behind things you see at home, in school, and outdoors in Kenya.

It is the space that has a watery fluid (cell sap) that contains dissolved water, mineral salts and waste products. Both plant and animal cells. Cell membrane. Cell membrane is a thin layer around the cell that holds the cell together. It acts like a fence and controls what goes in and out of the cell.

Therefore, the cell can take in substances it needs and get rid of waste products. Both plant and animal cells. It is a jelly-like liquid that fills inside the cell. Use the practice questions to test whether you can apply the idea, not only recall the wording.

### Worked example

A visking tubing bag containing a concentrated sugar solution is placed in a beaker of distilled water.

1. The tubing acts like a selectively permeable membrane.
2. Water molecules are more free to move on the distilled-water side.
3. Water moves into the tubing by **osmosis**.
4. The tubing becomes firmer/swollen as water enters.

This models how water can enter living cells when the surroundings are more dilute.

PAGE 7 OF 9: MAGNIFICATION OF CELLS

**Subject:** Integrated Science  
**Grade:** 8  
**Topic:** 2.1 The Cell  
**Subtopic:** Magnification of Cells

### Comprehensive concept explanation

Magnification of a specimen is the measure of how much bigger a specimen is when it is viewed through a hand lens or microscope compared to its original size. Magnification is usually expressed using “X” before the digits, for example, X2, X10 and X20. The X stands for ‘times.’.

It is a measure of how much bigger an object appears when viewed through a hand lens or microscope, for example X2 means the object has been magnified or enlarged two times or the image is twice bigger than the actual object. Keep the definitions precise, and notice how each idea connects to the example that follows.

For a light microscope, the final magnified image of an object as seen by the observer is the product of the magnifying power of the lenses that are used. These lenses include eyepiece lens and the objective lens. Use the practice questions to test whether you can apply the idea, not only recall the wording.

### Worked example

A light microscope has an eyepiece of $\times 10$ and an objective of $\times 40$. Calculate total magnification.

**Formula:** Total magnification = eyepiece magnification $\times$ objective magnification

$$10 \times 40 = \times 400$$

The specimen appears 400 times larger than its actual size.

PAGE 8 OF 9: MAGNIFICATION OF CELLS

**Subject:** Integrated Science  
**Grade:** 8  
**Topic:** 2.1 The Cell  
**Subtopic:** Magnification of Cells

### Comprehensive concept explanation

The magnifying power of each of these lenses is marked on the sides of the objective and eye piece lens holder. Understanding this clearly helps you explain the science behind things you see at home, in school, and outdoors in Kenya.

In a light microscope, the revolving nosepiece holds three different objective lenses, each with a specific magnifying power of X4, X10 and X40. The eyepiece lens further magnifies the image formed by the objective lens. Keep the definitions precise, and notice how each idea connects to the example that follows.

### Worked example

A light microscope has an eyepiece of $\times 10$ and an objective of $\times 40$. Calculate total magnification.

**Formula:** Total magnification = eyepiece magnification $\times$ objective magnification

$$10 \times 40 = \times 400$$

The specimen appears 400 times larger than its actual size.

### Visual model — plant cell (simplified)

```text
 |  |   (chloroplast)*    |  |
 |  +---------------------+  |
 +---------------------------+
 * chloroplasts in plant cells (photosynthesis)
```

| Lens | Example power | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Eyepiece | ×10 | Near the eye |
| Objective | ×4, ×10, ×40 | Near the specimen |
| Total magnification | eyepiece × objective | Final image size |
